claim: Platynereis dumerilii is a marine annelid (Errantia, Nereididae).
source: Platynereis dumerilii is a marine annelid (Errantia, Nereididae) suitable to address the questions outlined above.
evidence: This is a direct statement in the text describing the taxonomic classification of the organism.

claim: P. dumerilii is phylogenetically distant from clitellates.
source: As an Errant 'Polychaete', P. dumerilii is phylogenetically distant from clitellates (Struck et al., 2011; Weigert and Bleidorn, 2016)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published phylogenetic studies.

claim: P. dumerilii is presumably much closer in anatomy to the last common ancestor of annelids than clitellates.
source: As an Errant 'Polychaete', P. dumerilii is phylogenetically distant from clitellates (Struck et al., 2011; Weigert and Bleidorn, 2016) and presumably much closer in anatomy to the last common ancestor of annelids (Balavoine, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation and represents an inference about ancestral anatomy based on phylogenetic position.

claim: P. dumerilii has been suggested to belong to a slow-evolving lineage based on comparative genome analyses.
source: Based on comparative genome analyses, P. dumerilii has also been suggested to belong to a slow-evolving lineage, thus potentially bearing genomic ancestral features of annelids (Raible et al., 2005; Raible and Arendt, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to comparative genomic studies.

claim: P. dumerilii has externally fertilized, relatively fast-developing, transparent embryos which can be injected for lineage tracing.
source: In addition, P. dumerilii has externally fertilized, relatively fast-developing, transparent embryos which can be injected for lineage tracing and can be cultured at the lab for the full life cycle (Ackermann et al., 2005; Backfisch et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations describing the experimental tractability of the organism.

claim: P. dumerilii embryos develop into free-swimming planktonic larvae in about 24 hr-post-fertilization (hpf).
source: Embryos develop into free-swimming planktonic larvae in about 24 hr-post-fertilization (hpf).
evidence: This is a direct statement about developmental timing.

claim: By 48 hpf, segmental organization starts to become apparent in P. dumerilii, mostly evident by the repetition of paired bilateral bristle bundles (chaetae) on each segment.
source: By 48 hpf, segmental organization starts to become apparent, mostly evident by the repetition of paired bilateral bristle bundles (chaetae) on each segment (Fischer et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation describing developmental morphology.

claim: At 48 hpf, a mesodermal posterior growth zone (MPGZ) has formed anterior to the presumptive pygidium in P. dumerilii.
source: At this stage, a mesodermal posterior growth zone (MPGZ) has formed anterior to the presumptive pygidium (the posterior-most non-segmental region), juxtaposed with the four putative PGCs (pPGCs).
evidence: This is a direct statement about developmental anatomy at a specific stage.

claim: The MPGZ and pPGCs sit at the converging point of the left and right mesodermal bands in P. dumerilii.
source: The MPGZ and pPGCs, as a cell cluster, sit at the converging point of the left and right mesodermal bands, and both express Vasa mRNA and protein (Rebscher et al., 2012, Rebscher et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations describing the spatial organization and molecular markers of these cell populations.

claim: The first two divisions of ML and MR in P. dumerilii give rise to the pPGCs.
source: The first two divisions of ML and MR in P. dumerilii give rise to the pPGCs (Fischer and Arendt, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation describing cell lineage.

claim: The mesodermal bands and segmental mesoderm originate from the 4d micromere in P. dumerilii.
source: Previous studies show that the mesodermal bands, and eventually the segmental mesoderm also originate from the 4d micromere in P. dumerilii (Ackermann et al., 2005; Fischer and Arendt, 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous lineage studies.

claim: A pair of mesoteloblasts (ML and MR), similar to what has been observed in clitellate annelids, are active during P. dumerilii embryogenesis.
source: We show that a pair of mesoteloblasts (ML and MR), similar to what has been observed in clitellate annelids, are active during P. dumerilii embryogenesis and that they give rise to the mesodermal derivatives and pPGCs via asymmetric cell divisions.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on live imaging data.

claim: ML and MR give rise to mesodermal derivatives and pPGCs via asymmetric cell divisions in P. dumerilii.
source: We show that a pair of mesoteloblasts (ML and MR), similar to what has been observed in clitellate annelids, are active during P. dumerilii embryogenesis and that they give rise to the mesodermal derivatives and pPGCs via asymmetric cell divisions.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on live imaging data.

claim: A series of four contiguous primary blast cells produced on each side of the P. dumerilii larva proliferate to produce mesodermal blocks that each correspond to a distinct larval hemisegment.
source: A series of four contiguous primary blast cells produced on each side of the larva proliferate to produce mesodermal blocks that each correspond to a distinct larval hemisegment.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on lineage tracing data.

claim: M cells (ML and MR), after having produced the four larval segments, undergo an abrupt transition in their cycling behavior and start dividing much more slowly and symmetrically.
source: We show that M cells, after having produced the four larval segments, undergo an abrupt transition in their cycling behavior and start dividing much more slowly and symmetrically.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on cell cycle analysis using the live reporter.

claim: The final divisions of the mesoteloblasts give rise to cells that form the MPGZ in the early larvae of P. dumerilii.
source: These final divisions of the mesoteloblasts give rise to cells that form the MPGZ in the early larvae.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on lineage tracing data.

claim: The MPGZ cells remain in contact with the pPGCs in P. dumerilii.
source: The MPGZ cells remain in contact with the pPGCs, which are produced earlier and arrested in G0/G1.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on live imaging data.

claim: pPGCs are produced earlier than MPGZ cells and are arrested in G0/G1 in P. dumerilii.
source: The MPGZ cells remain in contact with the pPGCs, which are produced earlier and arrested in G0/G1.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on cell cycle analysis.

claim: Differentially-fated progeny of 4d (germline, segmental mesoderm, growth zone) display significantly different cell cycling in P. dumerilii.
source: We found that differentially-fated progeny of 4d (germline, segmental mesoderm, growth zone) display significantly different cell cycling.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on cell cycle analysis using the live reporter.

claim: The 4d micromere is the origin of mesodermal lineages and the germline in many spiralians.
source: 4d is the origin of mesodermal lineages and the germline in many spiralians.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about spiralian development.

claim: Embryonic segmental mesoderm forms via teloblastic divisions in P. dumerilii, as in clitellate annelids.
source: We traced lineages at single-cell resolution within 4d and demonstrate that embryonic segmental mesoderm forms via teloblastic divisions, as in clitellate annelids.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on lineage tracing data.

claim: Cell cycle regulation defines the correct timing and pacing of divisions for generating progenitor cells.
source: Cell cycle regulation defines the correct timing and pacing of divisions for generating the progenitor cells, as well as maintaining the potency of stem cells themselves (Ables and Drummond-Barbosa, 2013; Barker, 2014; Yasugi and Nishimura, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to literature on cell cycle regulation in development.

claim: Spiralians are a group of Protostomes including segmented worms (Annelida), mollusks, ribbon worms, and flatworms.
source: Spiralians are a group of Protostomes including segmented worms (Annelida), mollusks, ribbon worms, and flatworms, many of which undergo a stereotyped program of early cell divisions known as spiral cleavage (Conklin, 1897; Henry, 2014; Lyons et al., 2012; Seaver, 2014; Wilson, 1892).
evidence: This is a statement of established taxonomic knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Many spiralians undergo a stereotyped program of early cell divisions known as spiral cleavage.
source: Spiralians are a group of Protostomes including segmented worms (Annelida), mollusks, ribbon worms, and flatworms, many of which undergo a stereotyped program of early cell divisions known as spiral cleavage (Conklin, 1897; Henry, 2014; Lyons et al., 2012; Seaver, 2014; Wilson, 1892).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to classical and modern literature on spiralian development.

claim: Blastomeres that arise from spiral cleavage show determinate cell fates.
source: Blastomeres that arise from spiral cleavage show determinate cell fates and a strict correlation exists between cell division timing and cell fate determination.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about spiral cleavage.

claim: A strict correlation exists between cell division timing and cell fate determination in spiral cleavage.
source: Blastomeres that arise from spiral cleavage show determinate cell fates and a strict correlation exists between cell division timing and cell fate determination.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about spiral cleavage.

claim: The 4d micromere is an evolutionarily conserved blastomere across Spiralia.
source: The 4d micromere (also called M for Mesoblast) is one of the micromeres created during the fourth spiral cleavage, and it is an evolutionarily conserved blastomere across Spiralia (Lambert, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a review on spiralian development.

claim: In most spiralians, 4d gives rise to mesoderm, endoderm, and primordial germ cells (PGCs).
source: In most spiralians, 4d gives rise to mesoderm, endoderm, and primordial germ cells (PGCs) (Ackermann et al., 2005; Gline et al., 2011; Kang et al., 2002; Lyons et al., 2012; Meyer et al., 2010; Rebscher, 2014; Shimizu and Nakamoto, 2014; Swartz et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to lineage studies in various spiralian species.

claim: Within a given species, 4d follows stereotypical division patterns.
source: Within a given species, 4d follows stereotypical division patterns.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about 4d lineage.

claim: Differences across species in the 4d lineage division program have been proposed as a mechanism for obtaining the diverse body plans present across spiralians.
source: Differences across species in the 4d lineage division program have been proposed as a mechanism for obtaining the diverse body plans present across spiralians (Lyons et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation proposing an evolutionary hypothesis.

claim: Only a few studies have looked into the 4d lineage in detail across spiralians.
source: Yet, despite the immense diversity within spiralians, only a few studies have looked into the 4d lineage in detail, and some of these studies could not employ high-resolution lineage tracing due to techniques used (Fischer and Arendt, 2013; Gline et al., 2011; Gline et al., 2009; Goto et al., 1999b; Lyons et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to the limited number of detailed lineage studies.

claim: Very limited data are available detailing the relationship between the 4d lineage cell cycle characteristics and the resulting differences in cell fates.
source: In addition, very limited data are available detailing the relationship between the 4d lineage cell cycle characteristics and the resulting differences in cell fates (Bissen, 1995; Bissen and Weisblat, 1989; Smith and Weisblat, 1994).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to a small number of studies on cell cycle in 4d lineages.

claim: Annelids are characterized by repeated (metameric) body parts called segments.
source: Annelids (segmented worms) are a large but understudied group of spiralians containing many species with broadcast-spawning, giving large numbers of relatively small, yolk-poor and translucent embryos and larvae, which are amenable to functional developmental studies. Annelids are characterized by repeated (metameric) body parts called segments (Balavoine, 2014).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about annelid anatomy supported by a citation.

claim: In clitellate annelids, founder cells of segmental tissues are generated during embryonic development by stem cells called teloblasts.
source: In clitellate annelids, a taxon including the leeches and earth worms (Zrzavý et al., 2009), founder cells of segmental tissues are generated during embryonic development by stem cells called teloblasts (Anderson, 1973a; Devries, 1973, 1972; Goto et al., 1999b; Penners, 1924; Weisblat and Shankland, 1985; Zackson, 1982).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to classical and modern studies on clitellate development.

claim: Specific teloblasts make specific tissue types in clitellate annelids.
source: Specific teloblasts make specific tissue types.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about clitellate teloblasts.

claim: The 4d micromere is the originator of the M teloblasts (mesoteloblasts) that make the trunk mesoderm in clitellate annelids.
source: The 4d micromere is the originator of the M teloblasts (mesoteloblasts) that make the trunk mesoderm: the first division of 4d generates two bilaterally symmetric stem cells named Mesoteloblast-Left (ML) and Mesoteloblast-Right (MR).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about clitellate development.

claim: The first division of 4d generates two bilaterally symmetric stem cells named Mesoteloblast-Left (ML) and Mesoteloblast-Right (MR) in clitellate annelids.
source: The 4d micromere is the originator of the M teloblasts (mesoteloblasts) that make the trunk mesoderm: the first division of 4d generates two bilaterally symmetric stem cells named Mesoteloblast-Left (ML) and Mesoteloblast-Right (MR).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about clitellate development.

claim: ML and MR make the left and right mesodermal bands, respectively, via a well-described division program in clitellate annelids.
source: ML and MR then make the left and right mesodermal bands, respectively, via a well-described division program (Weisblat and Shankland, 1985; Zackson, 1982): the teloblasts repeatedly divide asymmetrically to self-renew the ML/MR stem cells and to give rise to tissue precursor cells (primary blast cells) through iterated divisions.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to classical studies on clitellate teloblast divisions.

claim: Teloblasts repeatedly divide asymmetrically to self-renew the ML/MR stem cells and to give rise to tissue precursor cells (primary blast cells) through iterated divisions in clitellate annelids.
source: ML and MR then make the left and right mesodermal bands, respectively, via a well-described division program (Weisblat and Shankland, 1985; Zackson, 1982): the teloblasts repeatedly divide asymmetrically to self-renew the ML/MR stem cells and to give rise to tissue precursor cells (primary blast cells) through iterated divisions.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to classical studies on clitellate teloblast divisions.

claim: Each primary blast cell follows a stereotyped program of cell divisions with fixed fate, generating clonal regions of tissues in adjoining segments in clitellate annelids.
source: Each primary blast cell (much smaller in size compared to the teloblasts they have split from) follows a stereotyped program of cell divisions with fixed fate, generating clonal regions of tissues in adjoining segments.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about clitellate primary blast cell behavior.

claim: Micromere 4d and its daughters ML and MR are evolutionarily conserved embryonic stem cells across spiralians.
source: Micromere 4d and its daughters ML and MR are evolutionarily conserved embryonic stem cells across spiralians (Lambert, 2008; Lyons et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to comparative developmental studies.

claim: The teloblastic nature of 4d derivatives in non-clitellate annelids has been suggested before but direct evidence for teloblasts outside of clitellate annelids is still missing.
source: Their teloblastic nature in non-clitellate annelids has been suggested before (Anderson, 1973b; Fischer and Arendt, 2013), but direct evidence for teloblasts outside of clitellate annelids is still missing.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations and identifies a gap in knowledge that the current study addresses.

claim: P. dumerilii has been suggested to belong to a slow-evolving lineage, thus potentially bearing genomic ancestral features of annelids.
source: Based on comparative genome analyses, P. dumerilii has also been suggested to belong to a slow-evolving lineage, thus potentially bearing genomic ancestral features of annelids (Raible et al., 2005; Raible and Arendt, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to genomic studies and represents an inference about ancestral features.

claim: P. dumerilii has three true larval segments with bundles of chaetae on each side and one cryptic anterior segment.
source: P. dumerilii has three true larval segments with bundles of chaetae on each side and one cryptic anterior segment (also called 'segment 0' [Saudemont et al., 2008], or 'segment I' [Steinmetz et al., 2011]).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about P. dumerilii larval anatomy supported by citations.

claim: The cryptic segment does not bear chaetae and is incorporated into the head of the P. dumerilii larva.
source: The cryptic segment does not bear chaetae and is incorporated into the head of the larva (Brunet et al., 2015; Fischer et al., 2010; Steinmetz et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations describing larval anatomy.

claim: mVenus-Cdt1(aa1-147) in P. dumerilii was present during G1 phase, and was then degraded, probably during S phase.
source: We found that mVenus-Cdt1(aa1-147) in P. dumerilii was present during G1 phase, and was then degraded, probably during S phase.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on time-lapse imaging analysis.

claim: The P. dumerilii Cdt1 reporter started accumulating again shortly before mitosis probably in late G2.
source: In contrast to the widely used hCdt1 reporter, which is specific to G1, the P. dumerilii Cdt1 reporter started accumulating again shortly before mitosis probably in late G2 (Figure 1B, see cell 'ab' and then cell 'b' before mitosis).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on time-lapse imaging analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: mVenus signal was present during mitosis in P. dumerilii cells expressing mVenus-Cdt1(aa1-147).
source: Consequently, mVenus signal was also present during mitosis (can be seen in Figure 1—video 1, Figure 1—video 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on time-lapse imaging shown in videos.

claim: Fluorescence was suddenly dispersed in the cytoplasm when the nuclear envelope broke down during mitosis.
source: Fluorescence was suddenly dispersed in the cytoplasm when the nuclear envelope broke down during mitosis (because the truncated chimeric protein, unlike the native Cdt1, does not bind to chromatin), and then quickly concentrated in the daughter nuclei when nuclear envelope reformed at the end of telophase.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on time-lapse imaging analysis with an inference about the mechanism.

claim: Contrasting cycling patterns were observed in sister cells in P. dumerilii embryos.
source: We observed contrasting cycling patterns in sister cells.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on time-lapse imaging analysis.

claim: 15.6% of cells were positive for mVenus, mCherry and EdU in P. dumerilii embryos treated with EdU for 3 min at 12hpf.
source: We observed that 15.6% (n = 51) of cells were positive for mVenus, mCherry and EdU, demonstrating that mVenus-Cdt1(aa1-147) was present during at least part of the S phase (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on EdU labeling experiments shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Only 2.1% of cells were positive for mCherry and EdU, but not mVenus, in P. dumerilii embryos treated with EdU for 3 min at 12hpf.
source: Only a few cells (2.1%, n = 7) were positive for mCherry and EdU, but not mVenus, suggesting that mVenus-Cdt1(aa1-147) was degraded at some point during the S phase (Figure 1D').
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on EdU labeling experiments shown in Figure 1D'.

claim: 75.3% of cells were found to be positive for mVenus and mCherry, but lacked EdU signal in P. dumerilii embryos treated with EdU for 3 min at 12hpf.
source: The majority of cells (75.3%, n = 247) were found to be positive for mVenus and mCherry, but lacked EdU signal (Figure 1D'').
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on EdU labeling experiments shown in Figure 1D''.

claim: Cells that were only mCherry(+) marking the early G2 phase made up 7% of all cells analyzed in P. dumerilii embryos treated with EdU for 3 min at 12hpf.
source: Finally, cells that were only mCherry(+) marking the early G2 phase made up a smaller percentage (7%, n = 23) of all cells analyzed (Figure 1D''').
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on EdU labeling experiments shown in Figure 1D'''.

claim: Ciliated cells in P. dumerilii larvae accumulated mVenus-Cdt1(aa1-147) once they stopped cycling.
source: As expected, we observed that they accumulated mVenus-Cdt1(aa1-147), once they stopped cycling.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on live imaging of differentiated cells.

claim: The mVenus signal reached much higher levels than in any cycling cell and remained at high levels in fully differentiated multiciliated cells in P. dumerilii larvae.
source: The mVenus signal reached much higher levels than in any cycling cell and remained at high levels in these fully differentiated multiciliated cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Figure 1—video 3 and Figure 1—video 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on live imaging shown in supplementary figures and videos.

claim: mVenus-Cdt1(aa1-147) is degraded toward the end of the S phase and is no longer present as the cells enter the G2 phase in P. dumerilii.
source: Taking into account that the vast majority but not all Edu(+) cells are also mVenus(+), this strongly suggests that mVenus-Cdt1(aa1-147) is degraded toward the end of the S phase and is no longer present as the cells enter the G2 phase.
evidence: This is an inference from the EdU labeling data.

claim: In P. dumerilii, mVenus-Cdt1(aa1-147) reporter is present during a larger portion of the cell cycle than the vertebrate reporter.
source: In P. dumerilii, mVenus-Cdt1(aa1-147) reporter is present during a larger portion of the cell cycle (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study based on comparison with vertebrate reporters, shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The mesodermal 4d micromere (also called 'M') gives rise to two symmetrically positioned sister cells ML (Mesoblast 'Left') and MR (Mesoblast 'Right') by symmetric cell division in P. dumerilii.
source: In P. dumerilii, the mesodermal 4d micromere (also called 'M') gives rise to two symmetrically positioned sister cells ML (Mesoblast 'Left') and MR (Mesoblast 'Right') by symmetric cell division (Fischer and Arendt, 2013; Rebscher et al., 2012, Rebscher et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The following two highly asymmetric divisions of ML and MR give rise to four small cells (1ml/r and 2ml/r), which have been suggested to form the germline (putative primordial germ cells, pPGCs) in P. dumerilii.
source: The following two highly asymmetric divisions of ML and MR give rise to four small cells (1ml/r and 2ml/r), which have been suggested to form the germline (putative primordial germ cells, pPGCs).
evidence: This is a statement based on previous studies.

claim: pPGCs become mitotically quiescent right after birth in P. dumerilii.
source: Thus, the pPGCs are the earliest lineage to segregate from 4d in P. dumerilii. pPGCs become mitotically quiescent right after birth.
evidence: This is a statement based on previous studies.

claim: pPGCs can be labeled with a short pulse of EdU around their time of birth (between 3 and 8 hpf), and be detected even days after EdU incorporation as they retain undiluted EdU while the neighboring somatic cells have largely diluted EdU through multiple mitoses in P. dumerilii.
source: As a result, they can be labeled with a short pulse of EdU around their time of birth (between 3 and 8 hpf), and be detected even days after EdU incorporation as they retain undiluted EdU while the neighboring somatic cells have largely diluted EdU through multiple mitoses (Rebscher et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: When embryos were treated between 5 and 7 hpf or 6 and 8 hpf with EdU, and raised to 24 hpf or 48 hpf, all four pPGCs were labeled with EdU in P. dumerilii.
source: We confirmed that when embryos were treated between 5 and 7 hpf or 6 and 8 hpf, and raised to 24 hpf or 48 hpf all four pPGCs were labeled with EdU under our culturing conditions (5–7 hpf treatment shown in Figure 2A for samples raised until and fixed at 24 hpf, in Figure 2B for samples raised until and fixed at 48 hpf; 6–8 hpf data not shown).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on EdU labeling experiments shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: When embryos were treated with EdU between 7 and 9 hpf, four out of six larvae had only two EdU-positive pPGCs at 72 hpf in P. dumerilii.
source: When embryos were treated with EdU between 7 and 9 hpf, four out of six larvae had only two EdU-positive pPGCs at 72 hpf (data not shown), indicating that pPGCs stop incorporating EdU around this time frame.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on EdU labeling experiments.

claim: pPGCs do not synthesize DNA between 11 and 24 hpf in P. dumerilii.
source: In addition, to test whether pPGCs synthesized DNA after they were born in the next 2 days of development, we carried out EdU incorporation assays after pPGCs were born, between 11 and 24 hpf (Figure 2C) and 24 and 48 hpf (Figure 2D). We did not detect any pPGCs positive for EdU in the larvae (n > 16) in either of these treatments, confirming DNA synthesis does not take place during this time frame in the pPGCs.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on EdU labeling experiments shown in Figure 2C and 2D.

claim: pPGCs do not synthesize DNA between 24 and 48 hpf in P. dumerilii.
source: In addition, to test whether pPGCs synthesized DNA after they were born in the next 2 days of development, we carried out EdU incorporation assays after pPGCs were born, between 11 and 24 hpf (Figure 2C) and 24 and 48 hpf (Figure 2D). We did not detect any pPGCs positive for EdU in the larvae (n > 16) in either of these treatments, confirming DNA synthesis does not take place during this time frame in the pPGCs.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on EdU labeling experiments shown in Figure 2C and 2D.

claim: pPGCs were mVenus-Cdt1(aa1-147) positive at 24 hpf and 48 hpf, suggesting that they are arrested in G0/G1 in P. dumerilii.
source: We found that pPGCs were mVenus-Cdt1(aa1-147) positive at 24 hpf and 48 hpf, suggesting that they are arrested in G0/G1 (Figure 2E and F).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on live imaging shown in Figure 2E and F.

claim: mVenus signal persisted in pPGCs after they were born in P. dumerilii.
source: Using the high-resolution time-lapse video, we were able to track the pPGCs, and observed that mVenus signal persisted in pPGCs after they were born (Figure 3A–H, Figure 3—figure supplement 1 for close-ups).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 3.

claim: pPGCs at stereoblastula stage were located on the external surface of the embryo in P. dumerilii.
source: pPGCs at this stage (stereoblastula) were located on the external surface of the embryo (Figure 3A'–A'', Figure 3—video 3, Figure 3—video 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 3.

claim: Soon after they were born pPGCs started moving toward each other, formed a cluster, and then moved toward the vegetal pole through epiboly in P. dumerilii.

claim: The movement of pPGCs continued on the surface until 20 hpf in P. dumerilii.
source: The movement of pPGCs continued on the surface until 20 hpf (or about 5 hr of imaging –Table 1) (Figure 3D'–D'').
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 3.

claim: pPGCs started to position internally after 20 hpf in P. dumerilii.
source: Then they started to position internally (Figure 3E'–G''), eventually assuming a postero-ventral position forming a bridge between the left and right mesodermal bands which converge at the ventral pole (Figure 3H–H'', 2E and F).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 3.

claim: pPGCs eventually assume a postero-ventral position forming a bridge between the left and right mesodermal bands which converge at the ventral pole in P. dumerilii.
source: Then they started to position internally (Figure 3E'–G''), eventually assuming a postero-ventral position forming a bridge between the left and right mesodermal bands which converge at the ventral pole (Figure 3H–H'', 2E and F).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 3.

claim: The trunk somatic mesoderm of P. dumerilii larvae is organized in three largely similar segmental blocks.
source: The trunk somatic mesoderm of P. dumerili larvae is organized in three largely similar segmental blocks (Brunet et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation describing larval anatomy.

claim: Each mesodermal segment is composed of identical left and right halves called mesodermal hemisegments in P. dumerilii.
source: Each mesodermal segment is composed of identical left and right halves called mesodermal hemisegments.
evidence: This is a statement of anatomical organization.

source: In clitellate annelids, ML and MR divide asymmetrically giving rise to an anterior to posterior linear series of smaller segmental founder cells called 'primary blast cells' (PBCs).

claim: Each PBC generates a metamerically iterated clonal mesodermal domain distributed over three consecutive hemisegments in clitellate annelids.
source: Each PBC generates a metamerically iterated clonal mesodermal domain distributed over three consecutive hemisegments.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about clitellate development.

claim: Each PBC makes 'one hemisegment-worth' of mesoderm in clitellate annelids.
source: However, each PBC makes 'one hemisegment-worth' of mesoderm (Gline et al., 2011; Weisblat and Kuo, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies on clitellate development.

claim: This stereotypic, anterior to posterior-oriented, asymmetric division process is termed teloblastic growth in clitellate annelids.
source: This stereotypic, anterior to posterior-oriented, asymmetric division process is termed teloblastic growth.
evidence: This is a definition of a developmental process.

claim: Progeny of each 'm' blast cell from 6ml to 8ml contributes mostly to a specific larval segment in P. dumerilii.
source: We found that, progeny of each 'm' blast cell from 6ml to 8ml contributes mostly to a specific larval segment: 6ml contributes to the left larval hemisegment 1 (Figure 4E–E'''', Figure 4—video 8, Figure 4—video 9); 7ml to the left larval hemisegment 2 (Figure 4F–F'''', Figure 4—video 10, Figure 4—video 11); and 8ml to the left larval hemisegment 3 (Figure 4G–G'''', Figure 4—video 12, Figure 4—video 13).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on lineage tracing shown in Figure 4.

claim: 6ml contributes to the left larval hemisegment 1 in P. dumerilii.
source: We found that, progeny of each 'm' blast cell from 6ml to 8ml contributes mostly to a specific larval segment: 6ml contributes to the left larval hemisegment 1 (Figure 4E–E'''', Figure 4—video 8, Figure 4—video 9)
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on lineage tracing shown in Figure 4.

claim: 7ml contributes to the left larval hemisegment 2 in P. dumerilii.
source: 7ml to the left larval hemisegment 2 (Figure 4F–F'''', Figure 4—video 10, Figure 4—video 11)
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on lineage tracing shown in Figure 4.

claim: 8ml contributes to the left larval hemisegment 3 in P. dumerilii.
source: and 8ml to the left larval hemisegment 3 (Figure 4G–G'''', Figure 4—video 12, Figure 4—video 13).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on lineage tracing shown in Figure 4.

claim: 5ml proliferates to give a mesodermal block located just anterior to the three true segmental blocks originating from 6ml-8ml and will possibly give rise to the mesoderm of the left cryptic larval hemisegment in P. dumerilii.
source: In addition, 5ml proliferates to give a mesodermal block located just anterior to the three true segmental blocks originating from 6ml-8ml and will possibly give rise to the mesoderm of the left cryptic larval hemisegment (Figure 4D–D'''', Figure 4—video 6, Figure 4—video 7).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on lineage tracing shown in Figure 4, with speculation about the final fate.

claim: Clonal blocks of cells generated by each blast cell were easily discernible at earlier stages of development in P. dumerilii.
source: These clonal blocks were easily discernible at earlier stages of development as well (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on lineage tracing shown in supplementary figure.

claim: At the final time point of the time lapse dataset (about 37.5 hpf), chaetal sacs had already started forming with a few elongating bristles evident in P. dumerilii.
source: At this time point, chaetal sacs (ectodermal structures used as anatomical markers of larval segment formation) had already started forming with a few elongating bristles evident, and each clonal mesoderm cluster from a single PBC overlapped with a pair of chaetal sacs present in each hemisegment (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–B',).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on analysis of time-lapse data shown in supplementary figure.

claim: Each clonal mesoderm cluster from a single PBC overlapped with a pair of chaetal sacs present in each hemisegment in P. dumerilii.
source: At this time point, chaetal sacs (ectodermal structures used as anatomical markers of larval segment formation) had already started forming with a few elongating bristles evident, and each clonal mesoderm cluster from a single PBC overlapped with a pair of chaetal sacs present in each hemisegment (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–B',).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on analysis of time-lapse data shown in supplementary figure.

claim: Spots marking the mesodermal lineage lie just beneath each pair of chaetal sacs within a larval hemisegment in P. dumerilii.
source: We found that spots marking the mesodermal lineage lie just beneath each pair of chaetal sacs within a larval hemisegment (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C–D''), confirming that these were mesodermal cells forming the layer beneath the elongating chaetal sacs at this stage.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on cross-sectional analysis shown in supplementary figure.

claim: Mesodermal blocks were initially beneath the elongating and deepening chaetal sacs in P. dumerilii.
source: Mesodermal blocks were initially beneath the elongating and deepening chaetal sacs (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A–B, Figure 4—video 17), but they eventually formed mesodermal pockets surrounding the chaetal sacs like sheaths (Figure 4—figure supplement 3C–D, Figure 4—video 17).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on time-lapse imaging shown in supplementary figure and video.

claim: Mesodermal blocks eventually formed mesodermal pockets surrounding the chaetal sacs like sheaths in P. dumerilii.
source: Mesodermal blocks were initially beneath the elongating and deepening chaetal sacs (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A–B, Figure 4—video 17), but they eventually formed mesodermal pockets surrounding the chaetal sacs like sheaths (Figure 4—figure supplement 3C–D, Figure 4—video 17).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on time-lapse imaging shown in supplementary figure and video.

claim: Before the chaetal sacs started to elongate and sink into the mesodermal layer, clear mesodermal segment boundaries were briefly visible, in the form of dorso-ventrally stretched cells in P. dumerilii.
source: Interestingly, before the chaetal sacs started to elongate and sink into the mesodermal layer, clear mesodermal segment boundaries were briefly visible, in the form of dorso-ventrally stretched cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 3C, arrows).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on time-lapse imaging shown in supplementary figure.

claim: In P. dumerilii, segmental anlagen become distinguishable at the transcriptional level already by 34 hpf, evident by the striped pattern of gene expression in the pre-segmental mesoderm and ectoderm.
source: Furthermore, in P. dumerilii, previous works have shown that segmental anlagen become distinguishable at the transcriptional level already by 34 hpf, evident by the striped pattern of gene expression in the pre-segmental mesoderm and ectoderm (Saudemont et al., 2008; Steinmetz et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous gene expression studies.

claim: 1ml and 2ml (1mr and 2mr for the right side) corresponded to the bilateral pairs of pPGCs in P. dumerilii.
source: We also looked into the fate of blast cells segregated prior to these segmental lineages. 1ml and 2ml (1mr and 2mr for the right side) corresponded to the bilateral pairs of pPGCs as described above (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on lineage tracing shown in Figure 4.

claim: pPGCs (1ml/r and 2ml/r) did not divide further and stayed in the immediate vicinity of the M teloblastic cells near the vegetal pole of the embryo in P. dumerilii.
source: These cells did not divide further and stayed in the immediate vicinity of the M teloblastic cells near the vegetal pole of the embryo.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on lineage tracing.

claim: 3ml and 4ml blast cells, unlike 5ml to 8ml, underwent a limited number of symmetric mitoses in P. dumerilii.
source: 3ml and 4ml blast cells, unlike 5ml to 8ml, underwent a limited number of symmetric mitoses.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on lineage tracing.

claim: 3ml and 4ml lineages drifted toward the animal pole in P. dumerilii.
source: These small 3ml and 4ml lineages drifted toward the animal pole.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on lineage tracing.

claim: The progeny of 3ml and 4ml may be giving rise to anterior-most non-segmental mesodermal tissues in P. dumerilii.
source: However, the limited information we obtained suggests they may be giving rise to anterior-most non-segmental mesodermal tissues (Figure 4—videos 2–5).
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on limited lineage tracing data shown in videos.

claim: The data support that ML shows teloblastic behavior and the progeny of mesodermal primary blast cells contribute to distinct larval segments similar to what is observed in clitellate annelids in P. dumerilii.
source: Overall, the data support that ML shows teloblastic behavior and the progeny of mesodermal primary blast cells contribute to distinct larval segments similar to what is observed in clitellate annelids.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study based on lineage tracing data.

claim: At the eighth division of ML and MR, cells 8ML/R and 8ml/r are generated in P. dumerilii.
source: At the eighth division of ML and MR, cells 8ML/R and 8ml/r are generated.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on lineage tracing.

claim: 8ml/r are the founder cells of the third segmental mesoderm in P. dumerilii.
source: As described above, 8ml/r are the founder cells of the third segmental mesoderm (Figure 4G, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Figure 4—video 16).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on lineage tracing shown in Figure 4.

claim: The 8ML and 8MR divisions were similar in all three samples analyzed (Samples A, B, C) in P. dumerilii.
source: We compared three separate individuals (Samples A, B, C) for the 8ML and 8MR divisions and found them to be similar in all samples (Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Figure 5—video 1, Figure 5—video 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on lineage tracing in multiple samples shown in supplementary figure and videos.

claim: At the time they were born, 8ML/MR were positioned immediately next to the pPGCs in P. dumerilii.
source: At the time they were born, 8ML/MR were positioned immediately next to the pPGCs (Figure 6U–U'; Figure 4—figure supplement 1; Figure 4—video 14, Figure 4—video 15).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on lineage tracing shown in Figure 6 and supplementary materials.

claim: By mid-trochophore stage (around time points 55–60), all individuals had three cells on the left and right sides near pPGCs in P. dumerilii.
source: By mid-trochophore stage (around time points 55–60), all individuals had three cells on the left and right sides near pPGCs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C').
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on lineage tracing shown in supplementary figure.

claim: Two of the three cells near pPGCs divided eventually (around the same time in the left and right sides, but not perfectly simultaneously) in P. dumerilii.
source: Two of these cells divided eventually (around the same time in the left and right sides, but not perfectly simultaneously) (Figure 5A'–A'''; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A''-C'') expanding the progeny of 8ML and 8MR to 5 cells on each side (10 total).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on lineage tracing shown in Figure 5.

claim: By the last time point of the datasets (corresponding to the end of mid-trochophore stage), 8ML and 8MR had given rise to five cells each that were surrounding the four pPGCs and formed a posterior 'bridge' between the right and left mesodermal bands in P. dumerilii.
source: Thus, by the last time point of our datasets (corresponding to the end of mid-trochophore stage), 8ML and 8MR had given rise to five cells each that were surrounding the four pPGCs and formed a posterior 'bridge' between the right and left mesodermal bands.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on lineage tracing.

claim: The cells derived from 8ML and 8MR were positioned slightly posterior to the pPGC cluster in P. dumerilii.
source: They were positioned slightly posterior to the pPGC cluster (Figure 5B–B''), in the region which has been previously described as the mesodermal posterior growth zone (Rebscher et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on lineage tracing shown in Figure 5.

claim: The cells derived from 8ML and 8MR represent the founding lineage ring of mesodermal stem cells that will be active later in juvenile development in the segment addition zone in P. dumerilii.
source: We thus suggest that these cells represent the founding lineage ring of mesodermal stem cells that will be active later in juvenile development in the segment addition zone (Gazave et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study based on lineage tracing and previous knowledge, with speculation about future function.

claim: The division asymmetry (based on cell size) for 4d's two daughter cells ML and MR has been previously described using bright-field microscopy only until the seventh division (7ML/R and 7ml/r) conclusively in P. dumerilii.
source: The division asymmetry (based on cell size) for 4d's two daughter cells ML and MR has been previously described using bright-field microscopy only until the seventh division (7ML/R and 7ml/r) conclusively (Fischer and Arendt, 2013), and the divisions after this were not possible to observe due to the limitations of this imaging technique.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study and identifies a limitation that the current study overcomes.

claim: The first division of 4d is equal, creating two sister mesoblast cells positioned bilaterally symmetrically (ML and MR) in P. dumerilii.
source: The first division of 4d is equal, creating two sister mesoblast cells positioned bilaterally symmetrically (ML and MR) (Figure 6A–B, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on live imaging shown in Figure 6.

claim: Most of the divisions of ML after the first division were unequal in P. dumerilii.
source: However, most of the rest of the divisions were unequal, as expected of teloblasts.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on live imaging.

claim: The first two divisions of ML and MR are the most unequal in P. dumerilii.
source: The first two divisions of ML and MR, are the most unequal.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on live imaging.

claim: The first two divisions of ML and MR gave rise to large daughter cells (1ML, 1MR, 2ML, 2MR) and very small ones (1ml, 1mr, 2ml, 2mr) in P. dumerilii.
source: They gave rise to large daughter cells (1ML, 1MR, 2ML, 2MR) and very small ones (1ml, 1mr, 2ml, 2mr).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on live imaging.

claim: Division of 2ML, 3ML, 4ML, 5ML were all unequal in P. dumerilii.
source: After the initial divisions that gave rise to the pPGCs, the mesoblast (now named 2ML) continued to divide, budding off small cells: division of 2ML, 3ML, 4ML, 5ML were all unequal (Figure 6E, G, J and L, respectively).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on live imaging shown in Figure 6.

claim: The size difference between the two daughter cells progressively decreased in ML divisions in P. dumerilii.
source: However, the size difference between the two daughter cells progressively decreased.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on live imaging.

claim: 3ml and 4ml were small precursors compared to the later segmental precursors, 5ml, 6ml in P. dumerilii.
source: This seemed to be due to the fact that 3ml and 4ml were small precursors compared to the later segmental precursors, 5ml, 6ml (compare Figure 6E and G with 6J and L) but also due to the gradual decrease in size of the remaining M teloblast.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on live imaging shown in Figure 6.

claim: Division of 6ML into 7ML and 7ml was roughly equal in size in P. dumerilii.
source: Following this tendency, division of 6ML into 7ML and 7ml was roughly equal in size (Figure 6O).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on live imaging shown in Figure 6.

claim: 7ML then divided unequally again, giving rise to 8ML and 8ml in P. dumerilii.
source: We observed that 7ML then divided unequally again, giving rise to 8ML and 8ml (Figure 6S).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on live imaging shown in Figure 6.

claim: The size difference in the division of 7ML was inverted: 8ml, precursor of the mesoderm of the third segment was the large cell and 8ML, the remaining teloblast cell, was now very small in P. dumerilii.
source: But, surprisingly this time, the size difference was inverted: 8ml, precursor of the mesoderm of the third segment was the large cell and 8ML, the remaining teloblast cell, was now very small.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on live imaging.

claim: The further divisions of the remaining teloblast 8ML are essentially equal and give a cluster of quite small cells in P. dumerilii.
source: The further divisions of this remaining teloblast 8ML are essentially equal and give a cluster of quite small cells.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on live imaging.

claim: 4d lineage shows asymmetric divisions similar to clitellate mesoteloblasts in P. dumerilii.
source: Thus, we confirm that 4d lineage shows asymmetric divisions similar to clitellate mesoteloblasts.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study based on live imaging data.

claim: Unlike in the leech, in P. dumerilii the mesodermal teloblasts decreased in size very rapidly through the eight-division sequence.
source: However, unlike in the leech, in P. dumerilii the mesodermal teloblasts decreased in size very rapidly through this eight-division sequence, and we observed a reversed asymmetry at the end of the sequence.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study based on live imaging data comparing P. dumerilii to leech.

claim: A reversed asymmetry was observed at the end of the eight-division sequence in P. dumerilii mesodermal teloblasts.
source: However, unlike in the leech, in P. dumerilii the mesodermal teloblasts decreased in size very rapidly through this eight-division sequence, and we observed a reversed asymmetry at the end of the sequence.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study based on live imaging data.

claim: The mesodermal teloblastic lineage (derived from 8ML/MR) that will presumably produce the segments of the juvenile starts from a cluster of very small cells in P. dumerilii.
source: The mesodermal teloblastic lineage (derived from 8ML/MR) that will presumably produce the segments of the juvenile thus starts from a cluster of very small cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study based on lineage tracing with speculation about future function.

claim: The orientation of divisions sequentially shifted in a clock-wise fashion for the left mesoteloblast divisions in P. dumerilii, when looking from the posterior pole.
source: As observed in previous work (Fischer and Arendt, 2013), the orientation of divisions also sequentially shifted in a clock-wise fashion for the left mesoteloblast divisions (Figure 6E, G, J, L, O and S, summarized in Figure 6V), when looking from the posterior pole.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on live imaging shown in Figure 6, confirmed by a previous study.

claim: The first series of precursors (pPGCs, 3ml, 4ml) were budded off roughly in the direction of the future blastopore in P. dumerilii.
source: Consequently, whereas the first series of precursors (pPGCs, 3ml, 4ml) were budded off roughly in the direction of the future blastopore, the later segmental precursors (5ml to 8ml) were budded off progressively more towards the anterior of the embryo, also reflecting the gradual change of size of the teloblast cell and its shifting position toward the vegetal pole.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on live imaging.

claim: The later segmental precursors (5ml to 8ml) were budded off progressively more towards the anterior of the embryo in P. dumerilii.
source: Consequently, whereas the first series of precursors (pPGCs, 3ml, 4ml) were budded off roughly in the direction of the future blastopore, the later segmental precursors (5ml to 8ml) were budded off progressively more towards the anterior of the embryo, also reflecting the gradual change of size of the teloblast cell and its shifting position toward the vegetal pole.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on live imaging.

claim: There is no 'segmentation clock' but a 'segmentation oscillator' of decreasing frequency in the P. dumerilii embryo.
source: This is not the case in P. dumerilii as the time interval increases gradually between divisions. Precisely, at the experimental temperatures 4ML, 5ML, 6ML, 7ML divisions happened in 30, 30, 40, and 50 mins after the preceding division, respectively. Thus, there is no 'segmentation clock' but a 'segmentation oscillator' of decreasing frequency in the embryo.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study based on timing measurements from live imaging.

claim: At the experimental temperatures 4ML, 5ML, 6ML, 7ML divisions happened in 30, 30, 40, and 50 mins after the preceding division, respectively, in P. dumerilii.
source: Precisely, at the experimental temperatures 4ML, 5ML, 6ML, 7ML divisions happened in 30, 30, 40, and 50 mins after the preceding division, respectively.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on timing measurements from live imaging.

claim: pPGCs stopped cycling after they were born in P. dumerilii.
source: pPGCs stopped cycling after they were born (Figures 2 and 3; Figure 3—figure supplement 1) and as expected, a roughly linear plot, without significant valleys and peaks was obtained for these cells (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on cell cycle analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The mesoblast ML had clear cycling with prominent valleys and peaks in P. dumerilii.
source: The mesoblast ML, in contrast, had clear cycling with prominent valleys and peaks (Figure 7B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on cell cycle analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Initially 7ml and 8ml sub-lineages are out of phase (valleys and peaks do not overlap) even though cycling periodicity is similar in P. dumerilii.
source: The comparison of 7ml sub-lineage to 8ml sub-lineage revealed that initially these two are out of phase (valleys and peaks do not overlap) even though cycling periodicity is similar.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on cell cycle analysis.

claim: By time point 46, 7ml and 8ml sub-lineages become synchronized as shown by the overlapping graphs in P. dumerilii.
source: However, by time point 46 they become synchronized as shown by the overlapping graphs (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on cell cycle analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: 8ml and 8ML sub-lineages differ from each other drastically: 8ML has much fewer valleys and peaks, indicating slower cell cycling compared to 8ml in P. dumerilii.
source: On the other hand, 8ml and 8ML sub-lineages differ from each other drastically: 8ML has much fewer valleys and peaks (Figure 7D, Figure 7—figure supplement 2A–E, Figure 7—figure supplement 1C), indicating slower cell cycling compared to 8ml (Figure 7D, Figure 7—figure supplement 2F–J, Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on cell cycle analysis shown in Figure 7D and supplementary figures.

claim: The cycling patterns are similar in different samples and in the right mesoblast in P. dumerilii.
source: We have also confirmed that the cycling patterns are similar in different samples and in the right mesoblast (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on cell cycle analysis in multiple samples shown in supplementary figure.

claim: The daughters of the blastomere 4d (ML and MR) produce the trunk mesoderm by teloblastic divisions in P. dumerilii, as in clitellate annelids.
source: Here we report techniques for long-term live imaging of P. dumerilii embryos and larvae, and demonstrate the feasibility of a FUCCI live-cell cycle reporter in this species. Using these techniques and tools, we reveal previously unknown characteristics of the development of this marine annelid, in particular the fact that the daughters of the blastomere 4d (ML and MR) produce the trunk mesoderm by teloblastic divisions, as in clitellate annelids.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion from the study based on lineage tracing data.

claim: Starting with the fifth division, each division of ML and MR gives rise to the mesoderm of one segment in P. dumerilii.
source: Starting with the fifth division, each division of this pair of cells gives rise to the mesoderm of one segment.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion from the study based on lineage tracing data.

claim: ML and MR give rise, by their two first divisions, to the putative Primordial Germ Cells (pPGCs) in P. dumerilii.
source: ML and MR also give rise, by their two first divisions, to the putative Primordial Germ Cells (pPGCs)
evidence: This is a primary conclusion from the study based on lineage tracing data.

claim: Starting with the eighth round of division, ML and MR give rise to the mesodermal posterior growth zone (MPGZ), which is part of the segment addition zone (SAZ) in P. dumerilii.
source: and starting with the eighth round of division, to the mesodermal posterior growth zone (MPGZ), which is part of the segment addition zone (SAZ).
evidence: This is a primary conclusion from the study based on lineage tracing data.

claim: The different cell types that originate from 4d (segmental mesoderm cells, posterior growth zone cells, and germ cells) show distinct cell cycle characteristics in P. dumerilii.
source: Interestingly, the different cell types that originate from 4d (segmental mesoderm cells, posterior growth zone cells, and germ cells) show distinct cell cycle characteristics.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion from the study based on cell cycle analysis.

claim: Long-term imaging at single-cell resolution for lineage analyses has been technically challenging in most spiralians including annelids.
source: Long-term imaging at single-cell resolution for lineage analyses has been technically challenging in most spiralians including annelids.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field.

claim: The micromere lineages (such as 4d) are small and very difficult to label individually in non-clitellate annelids.
source: The micromere lineages (such as 4d) are small and very difficult to label individually in non-clitellate annelids (i.e. non-clitellate Sedentaria, Errantia, and basal annelids) (Irvine and Seaver, 2006), as opposed to the leech and the sludge worm Tubifex (both clitellates), which have larger and accessible embryos that enable injecting single blastomeres to follow specific lineages (Gline et al., 2011, Gline et al., 2009; Goto et al., 1999a, 1999b; Storey, 1989; Weisblat and Shankland, 1985).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations describing technical challenges in different annelid groups.

claim: Some studies used DiI injections for labeling specific blastomeres and analyzing the domains they gave rise to in fixed samples, in which case there is no continuous observation by time-lapse imaging, thus no resolution at individual cell-level.
source: Some of the studies used DiI injections for labeling specific blastomeres and analyzing the domains they gave rise to in fixed samples, in which case there is no continuous observation by time-lapse imaging, thus no resolution at individual cell-level (Ackermann et al., 2005; Irvine and Seaver, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations describing limitations of previous methods.

claim: Other studies used bright-field microscopy for live observations, but only earlier stages of development could be analyzed as cell sizes become too small at later stages to confidently follow without any labeling.
source: Other studies used bright-field microscopy for live observations, but only earlier stages of development could be analyzed as cell sizes become too small at later stages to confidently follow without any labeling, and/or the larvae start moving due to ciliary band formation (Fischer and Arendt, 2013; Wilson, 1892 in two other nereidids, Nereis limbata and Platynereis megalops).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations describing limitations of previous methods.

claim: Behavior of specific lineages with detailed cell cycling characteristics at single-cell resolution could not be observed in previous studies of non-clitellate annelids.
source: As a result, behavior of specific lineages with detailed cell cycling characteristics at single-cell resolution could not be observed, and whether the lineages showed teloblastic activity in non-clitellate annelids could not be directly observed.
evidence: This is a statement about limitations of previous studies that the current study addresses.

evidence: This is a statement about limitations of previous studies that the current study addresses.

claim: Overcoming the long-standing challenge of immobilization of the trochophore larvae was particularly significant in this study.
source: Overcoming the long-standing challenge of immobilization of the trochophore larvae was particularly significant, because the larvae start spinning from 15 hpf and later actively swim via several ciliary bands.
evidence: This is a statement about the significance of a technical achievement in the study.

claim: The larvae start spinning from 15 hpf and later actively swim via several ciliary bands in P. dumerilii.
source: Overcoming the long-standing challenge of immobilization of the trochophore larvae was particularly significant, because the larvae start spinning from 15 hpf and later actively swim via several ciliary bands.
evidence: This is a statement of developmental behavior.

claim: Live imaging for extended time periods to follow cell lineages has not been possible in P. dumerilii larvae before this study.

claim: The DMSO treatment method for cilia elimination can be potentially applied to other marine ciliated larvae as well as freshwater ciliates.
source: Our DMSO treatment method (Materials and methods) for cilia elimination can be potentially applied to other marine ciliated larvae as well as freshwater ciliates (Balavoine, Özpolat, Duharcourt, unpublished results).
evidence: This is a statement about the potential broader applicability of a method developed in the study.

claim: Cdt1 cell cycle component in mammal and zebrafish FUCCI is restricted to the G1 phase.
source: Cdt1 cell cycle component in mammal and zebrafish FUCCI (fluorescent ubiquitination-based cell cycle indicator) is restricted to the G1 phase (Sakaue-Sawano et al., 2008; Sugiyama et al., 2009).

source: Our reporter mVenus-Cdt1(aa1-147) is not specific to G1, but it was sufficient to observe cell cycling patterns, therefore is a useful tool to study cell lineages and cell cycle dynamics during development of P. dumerilii.

claim: mVenus-Cdt1(aa1-147) is a useful tool to study cell lineages and cell cycle dynamics during development of P. dumerilii.
source: Our reporter mVenus-Cdt1(aa1-147) is not specific to G1, but it was sufficient to observe cell cycling patterns, therefore is a useful tool to study cell lineages and cell cycle dynamics during development of P. dumerilii.

claim: This is the first live-cell cycle reporter available in a spiralian model system.
